title: Regular pullback residue comparison over base codimension at most one
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and $h:Y\to X$ a regular morphism between Noetherian excellent schemes on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring, def-weil-flat-morphism, def-weil-regular-scheme, def-pc-scheme-fibre]. Here regular means flat with fibres that remain regular after every finite extension of the residue field. Let $\delta_X$ be a dimension function and $K\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$ a pinned potential dualizing complex [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. For a geometric point $\bar v$ above $\bar u$ put $e_v=\delta_X(u)-\dim\mathcal O_{Y_u,v}$. Define the pointwise pinning $p^h_{\bar v}:C_{\bar v}(h^*K)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda(e_v)[2e_v]$ by localizing at $u$, applying the canonical exchange $q^*C_uK\simeq i^!h^*K$ of [lem-per-regular-supported-base-change] for the closed fibre $i:Y_u\hookrightarrow Y\times_X\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{X,u}$ and its projection $q:Y_u\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)$, applying $p_u$, and then taking the inverse Gysin class $\operatorname{Cl}^{-1}$ of [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity] for $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(v)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{Y_u,v}$ on the regular fibre, as identified with the regular pinnings in [lem-per-prime-power-closed-immersion-gysin].

Let $\bar y'\rightsquigarrow\bar y$ be a geometric specialization of codimension $b$ above $\bar x'\rightsquigarrow\bar x$ of codimension $0$ or $1$. Suppose $e_{y'}=e_y+b$. Then the higher residue transition of [lem-per-higher-residue-transitivity] respects these two pointwise pinnings:
$$H^{-2e_{y'}}(p^h_{\bar y'})=H^{-2e_{y'}}(p^h_{\bar y}(b)[2b])\circ\operatorname{sp}_{\bar y',\bar y}.$$
The coefficient lines on both sides are identified by the specified specialization and its roots-of-unity transport. This assertion concerns arbitrary codimension in $Y$ but only base codimension at most one.

source.place: Expose XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.1 and Lemma 4.3.2.2, using Lemma 4.3.1.2: reduction by normalization of the strict-local integral base of dimension at most one, finite radicial pinning exchange, and the regular constant-sheaf case.

proof.text: For base codimension zero the specified geometric specialization is transport over the same point of $X$, followed by a specialization inside its regular fibre. Supported exchange identifies the restricted complex with $\Lambda_F(m)[2m]$, $m=\delta_X(x)$, and its costalk maps with successive supported restrictions. The regular-pinning clause of the prime-power closed-immersion lemma says that our inverse point classes are exactly the pinnings of this constant complex. On a connected local neighbourhood in $F$ these pinnings are potential by the regular-unit theorem. Factor the given fibre specialization into immediate arrows and transport; higher-residue transitivity gives compatibility for its composite, in any codimension. Etale and strict-local restrictions and the roots-of-unity transport used here preserve the residue maps by finite-Gysin residue covariance's locality clause. This proves the base-codimension-zero case, including identity arrows.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 4.3.1.1 and Lemma 4.3.2.1, fibrewise case; Theorem 3.1.2

proof.text: Suppose now that the base codimension is one. Replace the schemes by the compatible strict localizations at $\bar y,\bar x$ determined by the geometric arrow. The strict-local-model lemma preserves regularity, Noetherian excellence and the fibre local dimensions. The fibrewise pinnings restrict to the fibrewise pinnings of the strict-local morphism: supported exchange is compatible with this regular base change, and the point Gysin classes on the fibres are compatible with etale base change and strict localization by absolute Gysin purity. Let $C$ be the reduced closure of the lifted $x'$ in $X_{(\bar x)}$, and $i:C\hookrightarrow X_{(\bar x)}$. The prime-power costalk-reduction lemma makes $C$ an integral excellent strictly henselian local scheme of dimension one. Replace $K$ by $L=i^!K$ and $Y_{(\bar y)}$ by its fibre product $P$ with $C$. Supported exchange identifies $h_C^*L$ with the supported restriction of $h^*K$ to $P$, including successive costalks. For a closed immersion the finite-Gysin residue comparison is this supported identification; thus it preserves the original transition along $\bar y'\rightsquigarrow\bar y$, even when its codimension is greater than one. The pointwise finite pinnings on $L$ preserve every immediate residue square, by that same covariance. Hence $L$ is potential. The fibrewise pinnings on $h_C^*L$ are exactly the original ones: both are the composite of supported exchange, $p_x$, and the inverse point class, with the supported restrictions composed in the same order. We may therefore work over $C$, with the base arrow generic-to-closed.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.1, first reduction; Proposition 3.5.4 and Lemma 3.5.5

proof.text: Let $m=\delta_C(\eta)$. Since the base specialization is immediate, $\delta_C(s)=m-1$. Tensor $L$ with $\Lambda(-m)$ and shift by $[-2m]$, carrying the pinnings along. Supported exchange and the point classes commute with these operations; the residue comparisons do too. Consequently the desired equation for $L$ is equivalent to the equation for this normalized complex. We now use the notation $L$ for it, so its generic degree is zero and its closed degree is $-1$. The difference $e_{y'}-e_y=b$ is unchanged by subtracting $m$ from both endpoint degrees.

Normalize $C$ in its function field, writing $n:S\to C$. Prime-power costalk reduction says that $S$ is a strictly henselian discrete valuation trait, $n$ is finite and a universal homeomorphism, the generic field is unchanged, and the closed residue degree is purely inseparable and invertible in $\Lambda$. In particular $n$ is surjective radicial. It is excellent by finite-type stability of excellence. Form $P_S=P\times_CS$, with projections $n':P_S\to P$ and $r:P_S\to S$. Finite radicial base change and universal-homeomorphism base change give that $n'$ is finite surjective radicial. Finite-type regular base change applied on affine charts gives that $r$ is regular; its affine rings and those of $P_S$ are Noetherian since $n'$ is finite. Excellence follows from the same finite-type stability. The putative finite-detection theorem supplies induced pinnings on $n^!L$, which are potential because $L$ is. No use of the general finite-type potential-pullback theorem is made here.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.1, normalization square and Proposition 2.4.3.3

proof.text: The radicial-regular exchange lemma identifies $r^*n^!L$ with $n'^!h_C^*L$ preserving the pointwise pinnings specified on both sides. The unique lifted geometric arrow on $P_S$ has the same codimension as the original arrow, since the finite universal homeomorphism identifies their strict-local closures. Finite-Gysin residue covariance gives a commuting square between these two transition maps, with vertical maps the Gysin-normalized costalk isomorphisms $B$ at the endpoints. Conjugating by the pinnings therefore shows that the original transition is the identity on its normalized Tate line if the transition on $r^*n^!L$ is the identity. We have reduced the desired equation to this one arrow over the regular trait $S$. This is a comparison of the individual higher residue squares; it does not infer an individual square merely from a statement about global potentiality.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.1, use of Lemma 4.3.2.2 and finite detection; Proposition 3.5.4

proof.text: The dimension function induced on $S$ has generic value $0$ and closed value $-1$, so it is $-\operatorname{codim}_S$. The regular-unit theorem equips $\Lambda_S$ with potential pinnings for this function. Both $n^!L$ and $\Lambda_S$ are potential, and $S$ is normal integral excellent. Apply the uniqueness clause of the normal pinned-extension theorem to each: their pinning-preserving isomorphisms to its specified object give a pinning-preserving isomorphism $n^!L\simeq\Lambda_S$. The generic pinning is the identity after this identification. Ordinary pullback of this isomorphism respects the fibrewise pinnings, since supported exchange is natural and the fixed inverse point classes do not depend on the complex. Thus we may compare the pinnings of $r^*\Lambda_S=\Lambda_{P_S}$ with the canonical regular ones.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.1, replacement by the pinned constant sheaf; Proposition 2.4.2.1(c), or uniqueness in section 5

proof.text:
Work locally at an endpoint $v$ of the lifted arrow and put $u=r(v)$. The regular-map ascent theorem makes $P_S$ regular: its local coordinate maps are flat with regular source and regular fibres and Noetherian target. Localize to regular affine schemes $V\to U$ at $v,u$, and put $F=V_u$. Write $c=\dim\mathcal O_{S,u}$ and $d=\dim\mathcal O_{F,v}$. Regular base change of the closed-point immersion $u\hookrightarrow U$ gives a regular immersion $F\hookrightarrow V$ of codimension $c$ and identifies $r^*\operatorname{Cl}_{u\hookrightarrow U}$ with $\operatorname{Cl}_{F\hookrightarrow V}$ under supported exchange. The composite $v\hookrightarrow F\hookrightarrow V$ has point class
$$\operatorname{Cl}_{v\hookrightarrow V}=j^!(\operatorname{Cl}_{F\hookrightarrow V})\circ\operatorname{Cl}_{v\hookrightarrow F}(-c)[-2c],$$
where $j:v\hookrightarrow F$. The prime-power Gysin regular-pinning clause identifies the pinning at $u$ with $\operatorname{Cl}_{u\hookrightarrow U}^{-1}$. Invert the displayed product identity: the fibrewise pinning on $r^*\Lambda_S$ is precisely $\operatorname{Cl}_{v\hookrightarrow V}^{-1}$, the canonical regular pinning on $\Lambda_{P_S}$. The codimensions add, $\dim\mathcal O_{P_S,v}=c+d$, so the twist and shift agree as well. This proves agreement of the specified maps, including normalization, at both endpoints.

On a connected regular local neighbourhood of the special endpoint in $P_S$, the canonical constant-sheaf pinnings are potential by the regular-unit theorem. Compose their immediate compatibilities along any immediate factorization of the lifted arrow. Higher-residue transitivity says that the resulting map is its higher transition, so in the canonical pinning coordinates it is the identity in the unique nonzero degree. Step 7 identifies those coordinates with the fibrewise ones, Step 6 with those for $r^*n^!L$, and Step 5 descends this equality to $h_C^*L$. Undo the common twist and shift of Step 3 and the supported restrictions of Step 2. At the original endpoints the source degree is $-2e_{y'}$ and the target degree before pinning is $-2e_{y'}+2b=-2e_y$. Thus the equality is exactly
$$H^{-2e_{y'}}(p^h_{\bar y'})=H^{-2e_{y'}}(p^h_{\bar y}(b)[2b])\circ\operatorname{sp}_{\bar y',\bar y}.$$
All identifications are for the specified geometric arrow; the locality and twist clauses already cited keep its roots-of-unity transport fixed.

No SGA is used. The item statement is unchanged; the hypothesis e_{y'}=e_y+b is automatic at base codimension 0. Step checks: (1) base codim 0 works inside the regular fibre F (Noetherian, excellent, regular); its pinnings are Cl^{-1}(m)[2m] (closed-immersion-gysin clause), potential by regular-unit, and the higher transitions transfer by the closed-immersion clause. (2) The strict-local model and costalk-reduction give the curve C; L=i^!K is potential by 3.5.4. (3) Elementary twist. (4) S is a strictly henselian DVR; n is a finite radicial universal homeomorphism; r is regular by 07C1. (5) The exchange plus conjugation of the covariance square is correct (checked by hand). (6) normal-pinned-extension uniqueness gives n^!L≅Λ_S; no cycle (closure script, the item's only citer is regular-pullback-pinnings). (7) This is 4.3.1.2: regular base change of Cl and the composition Cl_{v→V}=j^!Cl_F∘Cl_{v→F}(−c)[−2c]. (8) Degrees: −2e_{y'}+2b=−2e_y. New nodes: radicial-exchange is 4.3.2.2 (tested with an E'/E purely inseparable of degree p; the degree is kept); strict-local-model is true clause by clause (ind-étale after a regular map, 06LJ, flat dimension count).
